name: Desiccated thyroid (Armour)

lead: Desiccated thyroid is dried animal thyroid gland that supplies both T4 and T3. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand.
It is prescribed for hypothyroidism, and some people discuss it for weight management; no trials support that use.

paras: The T4 and T3 in the extract bind thyroid hormone receptors and raise metabolic rate.
Batch variability and high T3 peaks are cited concerns. Excess doses can cause arrhythmias, anxiety and heart failure.

lead: Desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) is dried, powdered thyroid gland, usually from pigs, taken orally for hypothyroidism. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand.[1] It contains both T4 and T3, in a ratio of roughly 4:1 compared with about 11:1 in humans.[1]

It was the main hypothyroidism treatment from the 1890s until synthetic levothyroxine replaced it from the 1960s.[1][2] The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians recommend levothyroxine over thyroid extract.[1]

Some patients and prescribers prefer DTE, and it is sometimes discussed for weight management. Excessive thyroid hormone doses can cause weight loss but also fever, anxiety, arrhythmias and heart failure.[1] No studies have tested DTE as a slimming treatment in euthyroid people.

paras: George Redmayne Murray described treating myxedema with thyroid extract in 1891. Use declined from the 1960s as levothyroxine offered consistent potency, and a 1980 JAMA study found large variation in hormone content between preparations.[1][2]

DTE is used for hypothyroidism. Arguments in favour include inclusion of T3 and patient preference, while arguments against include batch variability, supraphysiologic T3 peaks and the risk of symptom-based high dosing.[1] An online survey of hypothyroid patients reported prominent dissatisfaction with levothyroxine therapy.[3]
Excess doses may cause weight loss, fever, headache, anxiety, insomnia, arrhythmias and heart failure; regular blood tests are recommended.[1]

A randomised, double-blind crossover study compared desiccated thyroid with levothyroxine in hypothyroidism[4] and a 2021 comparative effectiveness study examined levothyroxine, DTE and combination therapy.[5] Registered trials include a phase 2 study of Armour Thyroid versus levothyroxine (n=284).[6] No studies found of DTE for cosmetic weight loss.

timeline.event: George Redmayne Murray reports treating myxedema with thyroid extract.[1]
Synthetic levothyroxine begins replacing thyroid extract.[1]
